papers.title: Beta-Myosin inhibition in skeletal muscle: Impact of Mavacamten on the diaphragm
papers.abstract: The diaphragm, a primary respiratory muscle, contains nearly equal proportions of slow, Type-1 and fast, Type-II muscle fibers. Muscle fiber types - classified based on their shortening velocities and force generation abilities - are largely determined by distinct myosin II isoforms. Mavacamten (MAVA), a small molecule inhibitor of beta-cardiac myosin ATPase, is currently used for the treatment of obstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HOCM). Notably, beta-myosin heavy chain (beta-MyHC) is not restricted to the ventricular myocardium but is also expressed in slow fibers, raising concerns about off-target effects of therapy used to treat cardiomyopathic conditions. Given that nearly 50 % of the fibers express beta-MyHC in the diaphragm, we hypothesize that Mava may affect diaphragm muscle activity. Using an in vitro motility assay, we investigated the effects of Mava on native myosins isolated from rabbit diaphragm muscle and measured the velocity of actin and regulated thin filaments. Mava caused a dose-dependent decrease in myosin-driven actin filament velocity, with an apparent IC50 of 1350 nM. Importantly, this inhibition was reversible upon drug washout, indicating a non-permanent modulatory effect. To determine the drugs fiber-type specificity, we tested pure slow- and fast-myosin isoforms from the slow-twitch M. soleus and fast-twitch M. psoas. Both isoforms were inhibited by Mava, but slow myosin exhibited nearly 20-fold greater sensitivity than fast myosin, suggesting a potentially stronger impact on slow fibers. Interestingly, the slow myosin isoform showed even higher sensitivity to Mava than beta-cardiac myosin. Further mechanistic analysis distinguished two modes of action: (i) promotion of the OFF state of myosin, likely reducing a pool of active motors interacting with actin filaments, and (ii) modulation of the actomyosin biochemical cycle. Altogether, given the diaphragms reliance on both fiber types for sustained respiratory function, this off-target effect may impair respiratory performance in patients undergoing therapy, underscoring the need for respiratory function monitoring. The studies have direct implications for understanding the modulation of myosin function under physiological and pathophysiological conditions, as well as following pharmacological interventions.

papers.title: Nuclear quantum effects on ion permeation through the open transient receptor potential melastatin 7 pore: A continuum-electrostatics estimate
papers.abstract: We estimate how nuclear delocalization affects magnesium and calcium release from occupied wells in the naltriben-open pore of transient receptor potential melastatin 7 (TRPM7). We compare the equilibrium distributions of sodium, magnesium, and calcium in the same open structure and fixed continuum field. Thermal quantum states extend over nearby positions, so the ion can sample more than one local environment. For the divalent ions, the model combines a Gaussian test charge in the nonlinear Poisson--Boltzmann potential, spatial dielectric self-energy, and the free-energy cost of restricting a correlated first hydration shell. The hydration shell comprises the water molecules that directly coordinate the ion. In a constriction, the wall can block access to some of these water sites. The classical and quantum calculations use the same insertion energy, pore geometry, and axial diffusivity. The leading Wigner--Kirkwood correction for a smooth ion energy $U_i$ away from the wall is $ell_i^2left[nabla^2 U_i-frac{beta}{2}|nabla U_i|^2right]$, up to an additive constant, with $ell_i^2=frac{betahbar^2}{12m_i}$ for ion mass $m_i$ and inverse thermal energy $beta$. The length $ell_i$ is about $0.02,text{AA}$ at $310,text{K}$. At the point-ion magnesium basin, the refined centerline self-energy reaches $430,text{meV}$. Steric constraints also restrict water coordination at the $1.43,text{AA}$ constriction. At $310,text{K}$ in the primary extended dielectric box, the deepest wells for magnesium and calcium lie at $22.75$ and $11.00,text{AA}$, respectively. The quantum changes in mean passage time toward the intracellular and extracellular interfaces are $0.68%$ and $-0.66%$ for magnesium and $-0.10%$ and $16.12%$ for calcium. Calcium starts on the intracellular side of the constriction and must cross it to reach the extracellular interface. The preferred magnesium site is already on the extracellular side. A change in the dielectric boundary for magnesium or the ligand penalty for calcium can move the deepest well across the constriction and reverse the extracellular response. For comparison, the circular point-ion estimate for magnesium changes from $-37.4%$ and $-34.5%$ to $-8.9%$ and $-8.6%$ with a $0.5,text{AA}$ wall inset. In the circular reference, the largest local correction occurs at the intracellular widening and depends on near-wall access and axial sampling. Its influence on escape from the occupied well is small. In a separate screened two-ion benchmark, classical repulsion changes escape barriers by tens to hundreds of meV. Isotope substitution tests the mass dependence at fixed charge and chemistry. Together, the results show how pore geometry, dielectric response, and water coordination determine which local quantum corrections affect directional release.

papers.title: Optimizing environmental conditions for PALM imaging of the nuclear pore complex labeled with the photoconvertible fluorescent protein mEos4b.
papers.abstract: Green-to-red photoconvertible fluorescent proteins (PCFPs) are smart fluorophores used in several nanoscopy approaches based on single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM). To optimize the achievable spatial resolution and facilitate molecular counting in these approaches, PCFPs should deliver a high effective labeling efficiency (ELE). Here, to evaluate the ELE provided by mEos4b, a performant PCFP, we designed a constitutive Nup96-mEos4b protein fusion in the nuclear pore complex (NPC) of U2OS cells, and performed PhotoActivated Localization Microscopy (PALM) imaging of NPCs in fixed cells under different environmental conditions. We find that removal of oxygen improves the ELE by more than 20%. Overall, using HEPES as buffer in deuterated and deoxygenated water delivers the highest quality PALM images of NPCs labeled with mEos4b. These conditions should be beneficial for quantitative PALM or Minimal Fluorescence Photon Fluxes Microscopy (Minflux) experiments in fixed cells. We propose a photophysical scheme that accounts for the observed improvements in the absence of oxygen.

papers.title: GPU handling of OPC water in GROMACS: validation by protein folding and a 1.6-fold speed-up
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation is one of the core computational methods of the life sciences, used to study protein folding, receptor activation and drug binding in atomic detail. The timescales it can reach depend on speed, and running each step entirely on a graphics processing unit (GPU) is now essential for fast simulation. Optimal Point Charge (OPC) water, recommended for the ff19SB protein force field, carries its negative charge on a virtual site, and in GROMACS 2026.3 virtual sites prevent the coordinate update from running on the GPU. The GROMACS developers have recently added GPU handling of virtual sites to the development version as an experimental feature. Whether simulations run in this way agree with the established CPU calculation has to be measured, and no such test has been reported over microseconds or in a membrane-protein system of production size. We compared a modified build that handles OPC sites within the GPU update (Optimized) with the official release (Reference). The two builds placed the charge site with the same error (2.3 x 10^-7 nm) and gave relative force differences below 10^-6. In five matched pairs of 5-microsecond simulations, the Trp-cage miniprotein folded with both builds (three of five Reference and five of five Optimized runs; P = 0.44), and the folded ensembles matched. Both builds reproduced the density, diffusion coefficient, dielectric constant and second hydration shell that distinguish OPC from TIP3P water. In a 166,826-atom membrane system of the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor, residue hydration agreed between the builds (r = 0.99), and Optimized ran 1.57-1.66 times as fast as tuned Reference on two GPUs, with 87-97% of the time saved coming from moving the coordinate update to the GPU. In these tests, GPU handling of OPC sites gave a substantial speed gain with no sign of altered physical behaviour.

papers.title: Phosphate selectivity in XPR1 is driven by direct multi-ion competition
papers.abstract: Inorganic phosphate (Pi) is essential for numerous cellular processes, and its intracellular concentration must be tightly regulated. In mammals, phosphate efflux is mediated by the Xenotropic and Polytropic Retrovirus Receptor 1 (XPR1/SLC53A1), the only known mammalian Pi exporter. We and others have recently proposed that XPR1 functions like a Pi channel, with the protein preferentially conducting the H2PO4- species of Pi over HPO42-. While some studies suggest that XPR1 can conduct other anions, the molecular basis of XPR1 substrate selectivity remains unknown. Here, we use over 110 s of molecular dynamics simulations, together with free-energy calculations, to investigate substrate selectivity in XPR1. We show that H2PO4- (Pi1-) is preferentially conducted over HPO42- (Pi2-), and that Pi1- progressively outcompetes Cl- for occupancy of the transport pathway. Free-energy and ion-interaction analyses reveal that selectivity arises from two distinct mechanisms: favourable protein-Pi interactions and direct ion-ion interactions in the pore. This direct contact facilitates Pi1- displacement via the previously proposed knock-kiss-kick mechanism, whereas entry of Cl- is restricted due to the preference for water-mediated interactions. Simulations with additional anions show that XPR1 remains permissive to several monovalent species, including nitrate, bicarbonate and methanesulfonate, while poorly conducting the divalent anion sulfate. These findings suggest that XPR1 does not achieve phosphate selectivity through absolute exclusion of competing anions. Instead, preferential Pi transport emerges from substrate-specific interactions and competition between multiple ions within a relatively permissive permeation pathway, providing a molecular basis for substrate discrimination in XPR1.

papers.title: Behavioral Plasticity and Dispersal of Free Swimming Coral Larvae via Vertical Tracking Microscopy
papers.abstract: Coral larvae disperse and seek suitable sites for settlement while undergoing rapid development, making this period central to reef connectivity, recruitment, and recovery. Yet how the accompanying changes in larval morphology, ciliary activity, and swimming behavior shape dispersal remains poorly understood. Here, using vertical tracking microscopy, we follow individual Acropora millepora larvae over hundreds of body lengths at successive developmental stages while resolving body morphology. We show a developmental progression from buoyant rise to upward- and downward-directed gravitactic swimming, followed by weaker gravitactic alignment at later stages, accompanied by body elongation and increasingly structured ciliary flows. Integrating these kinematics into a minimal, data-driven model, we separate buoyant drift from active swimming and estimate the propulsion costs of vertical migration and lateral spreading. Buoyancy supports early ascent without propulsion expenditure, while the model predicts lower costs of descent and lateral spreading at late developmental stages. Simulations in fluctuating flow, assuming no flow sensing, predict that directed swimming weakens when flow-induced rotation acts on timescales comparable to intrinsic heading relaxation. Together, these results reveal how development reorganizes the physical drivers of larval motion in ways that may support the transition from dispersal to settlement, providing a basis for incorporating developmental changes in swimming into models of coral larval dispersal.

papers.title: Polymer overlap and the organization of enzyme activity in crowded solutions
papers.abstract: Macromolecular crowding shapes biochemical reactions in subtle ways, yet a general framework connecting enzyme activity to the physical properties of polymeric crowders remains elusive. Here we show that polymer scaling concepts provide a common framework to organize the effects of crowding on enzyme activity. Using dextran as a model crowder and fluorescence measurements extending beyond the initial-rate regime, we measure the time course of product formation upon peptide hydrolysis by a representative protease. Time-dependent analysis with a reversible kinetic model yields an inferred equilibrium constant whose dependence on dextran concentration collapses onto a common exponential curve after rescaling by a molecular-weight-dependent concentration. We show that the latter displays the same scaling law as the overlap concentration expected for branched dextran, linking quantitatively the reaction response to a fundamental property of polymer solutions. The common behaviour breaks down for the largest dextran at concentrations well above this scale, identifying the limits of the common scaling behaviour. Altogether, these findings suggest that polymer overlap is a general organizing principle for interpreting biochemical kinetics in polymer-crowded solutions.

papers.title: Predictive modeling of photoactivation, diffusion and adsorption in cell - The case of the optogenetic CRY2-CIBN system
papers.abstract: Strategies combining optogenetics and careful spatiotemporal control of photoactivation are highly promising to decipher the dynamical network of biochemical reactions taking place at the m scale in living cells. To improve the spatial resolution of such methods, the roles of various molecular processes, such as photochemical reactions, diffusion and interactions, need to be understood and quantifed. In this article we develop a minimal and realistic model to describe photoactivation, diffusion and surface-binding of optogenetic probes and validate it thanks to experimental results obtained with a CRY2-CIBN system. A theoretical description of optogenetic activation is implemented, based on the photophysics of CRY2 and on its binding kinetics to the membrane through light-dependent heterodimerization with its partner, CIBN. The cell cytosol is described as a closed reservoir of activable CRY2 molecules. Then, a series of photoactivation pulses of a focused laser beam are applied to activate CRY2 proteins, driving their relocalization to the CIBN molecules anchored at the plasma membrane. We examine both the recruitment rate and the spatial distribution of CRY2 molecules recruited after illumination with either propagative or evanescent light. We have estimated numerical values for the corresponding parameters and put into evidence the key role of the optical saturation of photoactivation. These findings establish a framework to further improve spatial control in optogenetic experiments.

papers.title: Sodium coordination at the Na2 site enforces ion-substrate coupling in serotonin transporter SERT
papers.abstract: Secondary active transporters use the thermodynamically favorable movement of an ion down its electrochemical gradient to drive substrate accumulation against a concentration gradient. For the human serotonin transporter (SERT), strict coupling between Na and 5-HT transport is essential for maintaining neurotransmitter homeostasis, yet the structural mechanism by which Na binding enforces this coupling is incompletely understood. Here, we identify an interaction network through which Na coordination at the cation site Ct2 (also known as Na2) modulates conformational change on both sides of the transporter. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that Na occupancy of Ct2 stabilizes specific interactions between residues in TM5, TM8, and TM1 that together gate aqueous access to the cytoplasmic and extracellular pathways. Disruption of this network through mutations at Ct2 residues Asp437 and Ser438, or at the TM5 residue Thr284, reduces the concentrative power of SERT and allows a constitutive Na conductance, consistent with uncoupled Na uniport. These findings reveal how structural integrity at and around the Ct2 site enforces obligatory Na-5-HT coupling and thereby sustains the thermodynamic efficiency of serotonin uptake.

papers.title: Koopman Analysis Reveals Collective Modes Governing Cellular Dynamics
papers.abstract: Living systems are complex nonlinear systems that operate far from thermodynamic equilibrium, and this nonlinearity makes their dynamics difficult to analyze. Several linearization techniques have been developed to address this problem, but most are local. Koopman operator theory is a powerful alternative that linearizes a system globally. Here we show that it not only achieves global linearization but also reveals collective modes that govern the dynamics of complex, out-of-equilibrium nonlinear systems. Applying the approach to whole-cell dynamical models, we find that these collective modes have physical and biological significance and relate to distinct processes in the cell cycle and in cell-state transitions. Collective and normal modes are widespread in many-body systems, particularly in condensed matter (e.g., magnons, phonons, hydrodynamic modes) and in macromolecular dynamics (e.g., normal mode analysis). By demonstrating that such modes also exist in cell-state transition dynamics, and in non-equilibrium nonlinear systems more generally, we offer a new theoretical-physics perspective on these systems. The collective modes separate into slow and fast modes. Long-term dynamics are governed by a few dominant slow modes that form a slow manifold of much lower dimension than the original state space. Thus, although the cell is a very high-dimensional system, its cell-cycle dynamics ultimately reduce to a low-dimensional space. Each mode comprises the coordinated behavior of groups of genes and reflects the structure of the underlying gene regulatory network. The modes can also be decomposed into terms that behave like damped harmonic oscillators, drawing an analogy between the modes of a nonlinear system and the normal modes of many-body systems. Finally, our analysis suggests that the dominant modes are closely associated with biological processes in the cell cycle, including mitosis, spindle checkpoint signaling, and DNA replication and repair.

papers.title: Ionic waves drive fluid flow by inducing spatiotemporal porosity variations in the brain interstitial space
papers.abstract: We develop a model of interstitial fluid (ISF) dynamics in the brain driven by traveling ionic waves. The cortex is modeled as a 2D porous sheet with an absorbent matrix. A prescribed 10% sinusoidal porosity variation induces mean flow of O(1) {micro}m/s, even without an imposed pressure gradient. Including perivascular spaces (PVSs) increases the velocity and pressure gradient, and yields volumetric flux through arterial and venous PVSs, with maximum magnitude of 2 x 10-2 {micro}L min-1 mm-1. We show analytically, in the large-wavelength limit, that the porosity variation enters the pressure field as first- and second-order corrections. We then simulate a physiologically realistic spreading depolarization (SD) wave, finding that the induced porosity variation raises the mean ISF pressure to 4 mmHg, which falls to -0.7 mmHg during recovery. SD yields a peak velocity of O(10-2) {micro}m/s and a peak flux of 3 x 10-3 {micro}L min-1 mm-1, and transiently stalls the PVS-driven flow. Although the SD wave produces a larger porosity change than the prescribed wave, it evolves slowly and drives weaker flow.

papers.title: Feasibility of methionine oxidation quantification in proteins through Raman and FT-IR spectroscopy
papers.abstract: The development of biopharmaceuticals poses unique challenges, with alterations of chemical integrity potentially impairing product efficacy and safety. Thus, oxidation-susceptibility of drug candidates is typically assessed by chromatographic methods, potentially coupled with mass spectrometry (LC-MS), which enable residue-specific oxidation monitoring but require high-resolution instrumentation, specialized expertise, and may introduce sample preparation artefacts. These constraints have raised interest in orthogonal, simple and fast methods to probe oxidation in native protein samples. Raman and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) have shown potential for detecting methionine oxidation, the most common oxidative protein liability. The aim of this work was to transfer the known quantification potential of cuvette-based Raman spectroscopy to Raman microscopy and evaluate its suitability for high-throughput screenings. Following several technical optimizations, this work shows that the detection of oxidation by Raman microscopy could only be confirmed for molecular methionine in solution and not for proteinogenic methionine. In contrast, liquid-cell FT-IR enabled solid quantitative read-outs of methionine oxidation in proteins. Under the investigated forced degradation conditions, the method showed good agreement to orthogonal LC-MS measurements utilizing the multi-attribute method (MAM). These findings position liquid-cell FT-IR as a potential rapid, low-volume screening tool for oxidation assessments in native protein samples, particularly during early-stage biopharmaceutical development.

papers.title: Investigating the critical role of serine in antimicrobial peptide binding to lipopolysaccharide
papers.abstract: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a major component of the Gram-negative bacterial outer membrane, is a potent endotoxin responsible for triggering severe host immune responses and sepsis. Understanding the atomic-level mechanisms governing how antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) recognize and neutralize LPS is essential for designing effective anti-endotoxin therapeutics. Here, we present an in silico investigation of the single-molecule interaction between Escherichia coli O111:B4 LPS and the cationic antimicrobial peptide GL13K, alongside two single-point mutants at position 9 (GL13KS9A and GL13KS9T), using all-atom molecular dynamics and umbrella sampling simulations. Consistent with experimental trends, mutating SER9 into alanine significantly alters peptide binding affinity to LPS. Surpisingly, removal of the polar character of serine leads to substantial changes in the interaction of the N-terminus with LPS via the loss of hydrogen bonding to stabilize a hook shape at the C-terminal end. In specific, while wild-type GL13K exhibits the strongest unbinding free-energy barrier, the S9A substitution changes the conformational landscape in such a way as to redirect the peptide's N-terminus from lipid A toward the core oligosaccharide and substantially reduces the unbinding barrier, whereas S9T maintains an similar affinity. Our work demonstrates the effects of distal mutations even in peptides on their binding and lays important groundwork for the development of peptide-based LPS inhibitors.

papers.title: From DNA Helicity to Structural Twist: An Undergraduate Laboratory Module for DNA Origami Design
papers.abstract: Precise control of nanoscale architectures makes DNA origami a promising platform for biomedical applications such as drug delivery, biosensing, and bioimaging. A key constraint in DNA origami design is that crossover placement must account for the helical pitch of DNA. For new learners, however, it can be difficult to understand how a DNA helical pitch affects assembled structures. Here, we report a hands-on laboratory module to teach undergraduate students about this fundamental helical pitch/structure relationship. A rectangular DNA origami tile is designed as a model system with its helical pitch varying from 10.5 to 10.84 base-pairs per turn. When the tiles are linked into a ribbon, the small mismatch-driven deformations of individual tiles accumulate into a global twist. The twist appears as characteristic kinks under atomic force microscopy (AFM). In a five-day pilot, three engineering students designed the DNA origami tile and used CanDo finite-element simulations to predict its deformations at different helical pitches. They assembled ribbons and used an intercalator, ethidium bromide (EtBr), to vary DNA helicity without changing the crossover layout. With increasing EtBr concentration, all three participants observed the ribbon chirality transition from right-handed to flat to left-handed conformations. By comparing predictions with their own observations, students gain a practical understanding of how DNA helicity governs DNA structure design.

papers.title: Conserved Vulnerability, Local Tunability: How Binding Proteins Read Ligand Fluorination
papers.abstract: While rare in nature, fluorinated compounds are ubiquitous in synthetic chemicals ranging from pharmaceuticals to agrochemicals, yet how proteins recognize these anthropogenic molecules remains poorly understood. Here, we use three structurally and evolutionarily divergent solute-binding proteins (SBPs) specific for short-chain dicarboxylic acids as a comparative model system to dissect the principles governing protein-fluorocompound recognition. X-ray crystal structures reveal that each SBP uses a distinct binding mode, ranging from backbone-mediated to side-chain-dominated hydrogen bonding. Despite their structural divergence, ITC shows that all three proteins exhibit a conserved vulnerability upon binding perfluorinated ligands: binding affinity drops up to 80-fold, or is abolished, across all three proteins regardless of fold or binding mode. In contrast, sensitivity to partial fluorination is locally tunable, with one protein even binding a fluorinated ligand more tightly than its non-fluorinated counterpart. Using X-ray crystallography, molecular dynamics simulations, and site-directed mutagenesis, we show that aromatic residues positioned near the ligand contribute to this tunability, capable of either penalizing or favoring fluorinated ligands. Together, these findings establish that ligand-fluorination sensitivity reflects a conserved chemical vulnerability layered with locally tunable, structurally encoded selectivity, providing a roadmap for predicting and engineering protein recognition of fluorinated compounds.

papers.title: Growth-law offset and efficient protein synthesis in fast-growing bacteria
papers.abstract: Growth laws refer to simple relationships between various cellular components and the growth rate for exponentially growing bacteria subjected to various environmental and genetic perturbations. The best studied among these is the ribosomal growth law, which refers to a relationship between the ribosome content and the growth rate under different nutrient conditions. This relationship is affine, which means a linear dependence on the growth rate plus a constant offset. This offset, referred to here as the "growth-law offset" and which is substantial in size, has been rationalized in terms of ribosome sequestration and protein degradation effects in the slow growth regime. These effects however cannot account for the sizable offset observed at medium and fast growth, where the efficiency of protein synthesis is predominant. Here, we use a simple effective model of translation to show that efficient protein synthesis in the medium to fast-growth regime does in fact require a substantial growth-law offset, on the order of that observed in Escherichia coli. Our key observation is that efficient protein synthesis requires a nonlinear relationship between non-sequestered ribosomes and growth rate, but in the medium to fast-growth regime this relationship is well approximated by the affine relation in the growth law, with the offset being necessary for the efficient balance between ribosomal and non-ribosomal proteins directly involved in protein synthesis.

papers.title: ATSASfold: a web server integrating AlphaFold models with ATSAS-based SAXS analysis
papers.abstract: Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) is routinely used for the structural characterization of protein monomers in solution, and computational prediction methods such as AlphaFold now provide accurate atomic models for most proteins. When a predicted model and the experimental scattering curve disagree, several refinement strategies exist, but selecting the appropriate one remains difficult, particularly for users without SAXS modeling expertise. ATSASfold is a web server developed to help analyse the results of SAXS measurements on protein monomers and select appropriate refinement strategies. From a provided experimental SAXS curve, ATSASfold performs primary data analysis, gives a general assessment of macromolecules shape, size, possible aggregation state and data quality. An AlphaFold-generated model is fitted against the SAXS curve and the agreement with the experiment is evaluated. In cases where the fit shows significant discrepancies, a machine-learning classifier trained on SASBDB depositions assigns the case to one of four categories, suggesting the most relevant ATSAS-based strategy for model refinement: fixed model fitting, rigid-body modelling, normal-mode analysis or ensemble optimization. When needed, a graphical interface allows the user to adjust domains or flexible regions of the protein before submitting the structure to ATSAS online for longer fitting jobs. After the fitting is completed, ATSASfold provides a summary of the results. The workflow was tested on examples from the SASBDB open web-databank. These use cases demonstrate smooth operation of the web server and show how ATSASfold can simplify the transition from SAXS data collection to structure-based interpretation.

papers.title: A Deep Operator Network to Predict Thermal Dose on Brain Tumors in MRI-Guided Laser Induced Thermal Therapy: with Synthetic Data
papers.abstract: Background: MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) provides minimally invasive option for surgical treatment of recurrent brain tumors. While patient-specific prediction of thermal dose distributions would improve treatment planning, no quantitative methods currently exist for this purpose. Although conventional numerical solvers are being widely investigated, these methods are computationally expensive and often limited by accuracy and reliability. Purpose: Here we propose DeepoLITT, a rapid and accurate model to predict quantitatively heat propagation in LITT procedures. This study represents the first phase of the investigation which focuses on training and validating synthetic datasets to test model,s accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. Methods: We built DeepoLITT on a branch-trunk neural network architecture, where the first branch extracts feature from tumor images, the second branch encodes laser parameters (power, duration, and probe orientation), and the trunk models the mapping from spatial coordinates to the resulting temperature field. To train and test the model, we generated synthetic datasets with different noise levels (0~20%) to mimic LITT procedures with two distinct laser probe types (FullFire and SideFire [Monteris, Inc.]) by a FEM (finite element method) solver. The dataset consisted of 400 samples, of which 90% were used for training and validation and 10% for testing. To evaluate spatial similarity of predicted thermal dose distribution against the ground truth, we employed Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and Hausdorff Distance (HD) computed on CEM43 (Cumulative Equivalent Minutes at 43 {degrees}C) isodose contours at thresholds of 2, 10, and 60 minutes. Finally, we evaluated the model,s inference speed with a representative image grid. Results: For the FullFire laser probe, the DeepoLITT model achieved temperature prediction error with average values ranging from 1.16{+/-}0.40% to 2.92{+/-}0.25%, and peak values ranging from 4.26{+/-}1.31% to 14.94{+/-}0.43% as data noise increased from 0% to 20%. For the SideFire laser probe, the model achieved temperature prediction error with average values ranging from 3.79{+/-}0.53% to 5.13{+/-}1.00% and peak values ranging from 15.18{+/-}7.15% to 20.75{+/-}2.84%. For thermal dose assessment, at the noise-free level for the FullFire laser probe, the model exhibited strong spatial agreement with FEM references, yielding DSCs of 0.96{+/-}0.02, 0.97{+/-}0.21, and 0.96{+/-}0.21 with corresponding HDs of 0.09{+/-}0.08 mm, 0.07{+/-}0.07 mm, and 0.06{+/-}0.08 mm at 2-, 10-, and 60-minute CEM43 thresholds. For the SideFire laser probe, the model achieved DSCs of 0.96{+/-}0.02, 0.97{+/-}0.21, and 0.96{+/-}0.21, with corresponding HDs of 0.20{+/-}0.31mm, 0.11{+/-}0.30 mm, and 0.15{+/-}0.31 mm, respectively. As the noise level increases, these DSC values show a decreasing trend, and the HD values increase. In terms of computational efficiency, the DeepoLITT model inferences temperature maps with 0.04{+/-}0.05 seconds per 3D sample ([31 x 31 x 3] grid), compared to 24.32{+/-}2.12 seconds required by the FEM solver. Conclusions: The study with synthetic data demonstrates the proposed model is an accurate and rapid method in predicting thermal dose. After testing clinical data, the method has high feasibility to be deployed in real clinical environment.

papers.title: Beyond Linear Paths: Generalized Interpolation for Flow-Based Generative Modeling
papers.abstract: Flow-based generative models learn to transform random noise into molecular conformations by following a prescribed interpolation path between the two. Straight-line (linear) interpolation is the usual choice, but it is only one of many possible paths. We compare four paths within a single affine framework, xt = tx+ {beta}tz : linear, trigonometric, spherical and a new operator-based path in which each degree of freedom follows its own schedule. Linear interpolation is a limiting case of both the operator-based and spherical paths. The operator-based path bends inside it (contracted), whereas the trigonometric and spherical paths bend outside it (expanded). We train the same Transformer velocity field with each path on a three-well potential, the mini-protein Trp-cage and the intrinsically disordered protein -synuclein. All four paths reproduce the reference distributions with comparable accuracy, but they get there differently. The trigonometric and spherical paths resolve conformational basins early and approach the reference smoothly. The operator-based path delays part of the transport, so some features stall or briefly diverge before converging sharply. An exact relation between the rate of change of the KL divergence and the alignment of the learned velocity with the score difference, together with closed-form moments of each path, explains these differences. The choice of interpolation path therefore controls how a flow model converges, not only where it ends.

papers.title: A hybrid biophysical-neural network model links nanoscale cardiac junctions to tissue conduction
papers.abstract: Nanoscale structure of the intercalated disk (ID) governs cardiac conduction through gap junctions and ephaptic interactions and is remodeled in arrhythmogenic disease. Computationally expensive models that resolve ID nanostructure have been confined to cables of tens of cells, such that the role of ID nanostructure on conduction has not been testable. Here, we show that a hybrid biophysical-neural network model removes this limit. A memory-based flow map, trained on finite element method (FEM) simulations of single junctions and short cables, defines surrogates that replace each junction in tissue. The hybrid model reproduces action potentials with 1-2 mV RMSE and conduction velocity restitution across multiple ID geometries with a mean error of 0.24%. Without retraining, surrogate models run in 2-D and 3-D tissues, with over one million junctions, 10^4-10^5 times faster than the FEM model and within an order of magnitude of a monodomain model that neglects ID structure. In large tissues with reduced gap-junctional coupling, regional cleft widening blocks conduction, whereas either change alone does not, linking ID remodeling to arrhythmogenic substrate.

papers.title: Quantification of Spin Fluctuations during Stem Cell Differentiation Using Diamond Nanopillars
papers.abstract: Quantitative detection of radical-associated magnetic activity in living cells remains challenging because variations between quantum sensors complicate direct comparisons of intracellular environments. Here, we demonstrate a label-free quantum sensing platform based on substrate-fixed diamond nanopillars containing individually addressable nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers. The fixed architecture enables one-to-one measurements using identical NV sensors in the presence and absence of cells, minimizing sensor-to-sensor variability and allowing reliable assessment of cellular contributions to spin decoherence. Cellular compatibility assays supported preserved metabolic activity, DNA synthesis, and membrane integrity without detectable apoptotic activation. Intracellular NV centers retained approximately 10% optically detected magnetic resonance contrast, 20% Rabi contrast, and a Hahn-echo coherence time T2 of approximately 3 {micro}s. Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill dynamical decoupling extended intracellular T2 to 25.8 {+/-} 4.90 {micro}s. We applied this platform to embryonic stem (ES) cells undergoing doxycycline-induced differentiation toward the trophectoderm lineage. Identical NV sensors exhibited consistent coherence recovery following removal of differentiation-induced cells, whereas undifferentiated controls showed no systematic recovery. Calibration using the stable radical TEMPOL, supported by magnetic-noise modeling and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations, enabled numerical evaluation of local magnetic responses as model-dependent TEMPOL-equivalent spin densities of 0.084-0.567 spins/nm3 across different sensing sites. These findings establish a quantitative approach to investigating intracellular physicochemical changes during stem-cell differentiation and demonstrate the potential of quantum sensing to study biological processes relevant to tissue development and regenerative medicine.

papers.title: AmberMeta: From AMBER Simulation Files to Checked Protocols and FAIR Metadata
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) projects with AMBER often consist of hundreds of runs, and their history is recorded only in the files of these runs. Errors such as a run restarted from the wrong file, a missing or unfinished segment, or a replica that stopped early can therefore pass unnoticed into analyses, Methods sections, and data repositories. Here, we developed AmberMeta, a Python tool that reconstructs the simulation protocol of a finished AMBER project from its files as a draft for the user to review. AmberMeta then checks the reviewed history against the AMBER run outputs and writes a machine-readable record of the runs. This record can serve as findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR) metadata of the simulations, for example for databases such as MDDB or for annotation with ontologies such as MOLSIM, and as the factual basis of a Methods section. In 19 in-house projects, some of them still in progress, AmberMeta reported unfinished runs, replicas at different stages of completion, and runs whose files were not collected with them. In copies of eight projects, it reported 146 of 152 deliberately introduced errors. AmberMeta thus helps improve the reliability, reproducibility, and FAIR data management of AMBER simulations by providing a systematic, file-based record of what was actually simulated.

papers.title: Phosphorylation elicits bifurcated regulation of NaV1.5 by intracellular auxiliary proteins
papers.abstract: The cardiac sodium channel Nav1.5 carries the upstroke of the cardiac action potential, and its inactivation needs to be precisely controlled: shifts of only a few millivolts in steady-state inactivation (SSI), or incomplete pore closure generating a late current, are arrhythmogenic. Inactivation is modulated by both tyrosine phosphorylation and protein-protein interactions, but whether or how the two intersect is unclear. Combining protein semi-synthesis with electrophysiology, biochemistry, fluorometry and molecular dynamics simulations, we control phosphorylation at Y1495 in the DIII-DIV linker and demonstrate how it governs regulation by intracellular fibroblast growth factor homologous factors (iFGFs). We find that iFGFs act through two separable mechanisms: a depolarizing SSI shift of around 16 mV that is switched off by phosphorylation, and a suppression of late current that proceeds regardless of phosphorylation. Only the former requires an intact C-terminal domain/DIII-DIV linker interaction, and both differ between iFGF isoforms. Phosphorylation at Y1495 therefore does not switch off the iFGF interaction but instead redirects its output. Together, this reveals a mode of ion channel regulation in which a single post-translational modification selects between different functional consequences of a protein-protein interaction.

papers.title: UBQLN2, but not an ALS-linked variant, protects client protein from temperature-induced self-association
papers.abstract: Aside from its established role in delivering ubiquitinated substrates for degradation, the proteasomal shuttle factor UBQLN2 also functions as a chaperone, likely via its central STI1 domains. Chaperone activity remains poorly understood due to the lack of known clients. Domesticated retrotransposon protein RTL8 was recently identified as a UBQLN2 interactor, and RTL8's cellular levels are stabilized by UBQLN2. RTL8 is a small protein comprising an N-terminal helix that drives its high-order oligomerization and a C-terminal helical bundle that weakly self-associates, especially at higher temperatures. Here, we provide direct evidence that UBQLN2 acts as a chaperone for RTL8. The N-terminal region of UBQLN2, through its UBL and STI1-I domains, engages RTL8 with low-nanomolar affinity in a sandwich conformation that prevents temperature-dependent self-association of RTL8. Notably, an ALS-linked mutation in the UBQLN2 STI1-I domain reduces RTL8 affinity by an order of magnitude, and impairs the ability of UBQLN2 to protect RTL8 from self-association in vitro and to stabilize RTL8 levels in cells. These findings expand the functional repertoire of UBQLN2 beyond proteasomal shuttling and link its chaperone activity to a disease-relevant mutation.

papers.title: Matrix mechanics gate the expression of spontaneous polarity in multicellular aggregates
papers.abstract: Multicellular aggregates are initially spherical, yet tissues routinely break this symmetry to form protrusions, invade, and migrate. Whether this symmetry breaking originates within the aggregate or is imposed by its surroundings remains unclear. Here, we embed human mesenchymal stem cell (hMSC) spheroids in synthetic poly(ethylene glycol) hydrogels in which stiffness, viscoelasticity, and degradability are controlled independently. Spheroids in elastic matrices remain spherical; viscoelasticity permits symmetry breaking only in compliant networks, whereas proteolytic degradability permits it in both compliant and rigid matrices. Brillouin microscopy shows that symmetry breaking is accompanied by softening of the spheroid core and loss of internal radial symmetry. Three-dimensional traction force microscopy reveals that the force field is polarised even in spheroids that remain spherical: tractions concentrate at two approximately opposing poles, and focal adhesions adopt a similar bipolar distribution. In spheroids that do break symmetry, protrusions emerge opposite the pole of highest traction. A continuum model shows that an anisotropic distribution of contractile cells is sufficient to reproduce both the patterns and magnitude of the measured displacements. Force polarity is therefore an intrinsic property of the aggregate, whereas matrix mechanics act as a filter that determines whether this polarity is expressed as symmetry breaking.

papers.title: Amperometric reconstruction favors a toroidal fusion pore during kiss-and-run release of serotonin
papers.abstract: Kiss-and-run amperometric currents reveal the opening and closing cycle of the fusion pore. This study uses such information along with mathematical approaches to test whether the pore is toroidal or cylindrical. Individual kiss-and-run amperometric currents from serotonin release by leech Retzius neurons were used to reconstruct either a toroid of fixed rim curvature or a cylinder of fixed length. Two pieces of information from the companion paper feed the equations: the peak pore diameter, calculated from the number of hydrated serotonin molecules released at the current peak, and the estimate of the quantal number of molecules in each event. Another essential parameter was the diffusion coefficient of serotonin, which interacts with structural parameters to determine the channel dynamics. With literature values for rim curvature (7.5 nm) and cylinder length (15 nm) and D value calibrated on the median event, both geometries predicted peak diameters of 2.1-3.5 nm, each requiring its own D (7.7% and 21.1% of the free value). Diameter scaled with resistance, with a larger exponent for the toroid (0.63 versus 0.53), indicating that toroidal pores rose more slowly and closed faster than cylindrical pores. Finding a D value common to both geometries left the toroid almost unchanged but shortened the cylinder to 4.1 nm, about the thickness of one bilayer. Our data favor a toroidal pore of fixed rim curvature as the structure that releases serotonin during kiss-and-run exocytosis. The short cylinder may represent the nascent pore through a hemifusion diaphragm.

papers.title: Gene-scale DNA and chromatin ensembles with atomic resolution
papers.abstract: The spatial organization of cellular DNA extends across a wide range of scales, from sequence-dependent base pairing to the packaging of meter-long cellular DNA into micron-size nuclei. Integrating the information from disparate experiments, molecular simulations, and theoretical models into a coherent picture of DNA and chromatin organization across scales remains challenging. Here, we introduce hierarchical chain growth for DNA (HCG-DNA) to build atomically detailed ensembles of double-stranded DNA and chromatin. Starting from complete tetranucleotide fragment libraries encoding local sequence-dependent conformations, we assemble structures of DNA up to the megabase scale at quasilinear computational cost. From HCG-DNA, the large-scale polymer elastic properties emerge, in particular the persistence length. HCG-DNA recovers electron spin resonance, atomic force microscopy, and single-molecule force spectroscopy measurements of DNA structure across scales. HCG-DNA includes nucleosomes to generate 3D atomistic chromatin ensembles constrained by cryo-electron tomography or genomic nucleosome maps. With HCG-DNA, we show how small changes in nucleosome linker length alter nucleosome packing and chromatin compaction. HCG-DNA connects atomic-level DNA and nucleosome structure to chromosome-scale spatial organization, while providing scalable ensembles for coarse-grained model development and AI training.

papers.title: Structural basis of cage assembly by a bacterial flotillin
papers.abstract: Flotillins organize membrane microdomains implicated in signaling, cell-wall synthesis, and antibiotic resistance, yet how bacterial flotillins assemble remains unknown. Here, we report a 3.1 [A] cryo-EM structure of the Escherichia coli flotillin YqiK, purified through its NfeD-family partner YqiJ - the first high-resolution structure of a bacterial flotillin assembly. YqiK forms a membrane assembly of 54 identical subunits. Unlike human flotillin cages, which contain two alternating paralogues, YqiK assembles from a single transmembrane protein. The cage is ~38 nm wide and encloses ~900 nm2 of membrane within its ring of 54 transmembrane helices. Its wall helices run continuously for ~287 &Aring, the longest in any SPFH assembly, making this the largest membrane-anchored SPFH cage reported to date. In YqiK, helix length and tilt set cage dimensions, while intersubunit salt bridges and hydrophobic interactions stabilize the assembly. Focused classification revealed local discontinuities in the cage wall, suggesting possible conformational flexibility. Mass spectrometry identified stress-associated membrane proteins and respiratory complexes that co-purify with YqiK-YqiJ. Together, these findings reveal how a bacterial flotillin builds a large membrane-associated scaffold and provide a structural basis for investigating how such compartments organize membrane proteins within the microdomain they define.

papers.title: CircDNA-PAINT: high-resolution binary-barcode multiplexing with circular DNA docking strands
papers.abstract: Understanding key biological processes governed by cell surface protein distribution requires highly multiplexed imaging. Binary barcode methods based on DNA hybridization represent a powerful approach to such imaging; however, higher multiplexing demands longer DNA barcodes, which substantially compromise localization resolution. Here we introduce circular DNA-based multiplexed DNA-PAINT (CircDNA-PAINT), a method that achieves a resolution better than 20 nm and thus enables robust binary encoded multiplexing. This approach avoids the linear time overhead of adaptor-cycling DNA-PAINT and greatly shortens acquisition time for large-plex imaging. CircDNA-PAINT provides a new tool for dissecting complex nanoscale cellular architectures.

papers.title: Rapid screening of target-specific isotope labeling protocols for in situ NMR of bacterial membrane proteins
papers.abstract: We describe an approach for the efficient development of targeted isotope labeling protocols leading to nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) structural studies of bacterial membrane proteins in intact cells and native outer membrane (OM) vesicles (OMVs). The assay relies on the bioorthogonal non-canonical amino acid tagging (BONCAT) approach for metabolic incorporation of an azide-bearing residue, followed by copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) to an alkyne-functionalized fluorescent dye. Fluorescence detection in SDS-PAGE provides a rapid way to test samples for off-target background signal from endogenous proteins, bypassing the need for intensive NMR screening experiments. Using this approach, we develop an optimized protocol that enables high-resolution NMR spectra to be obtained in situ with negligible background signal. The BONCAT approach also enables target-specific fluorescence or nano-gold labeling of proteins at the OM surface, further extending the utility of this protocol for correlative structure-activity studies of membrane proteins in situ.
